title: Does Deterministic Generate–Validate–Repair Reduce Unsafe LLM‑Generated Network Changes? A Confirmatory Paired Study
abstract: We preregistered and executed a sealed paired confirmatory study (n = 200 intent→configuration tasks) to test whether a deterministic generate–validate–repair (GVR) pipeline that consults a deterministic NetOps validator reduces validator‑detected unsafe or semantically incorrect network changes relative to an LLM‑only generation pipeline. The study used a single hosted model (gpt‑5‑mini) under adapter‑enforced shared‑initial generation semantics and a primary deterministic validator. Execution completed all planned pairs (200 pairs). Every initial candidate passed the validator so no repair calls occurred: paired contingency n11 = 200, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0; estimate = 0.0; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0; bootstrap 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0] (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729). Because baseline validator failures were absent on this curated task bank under the frozen shared‑initial policy, the preregistered ≥50% relative‑reduction hypothesis could not be meaningfully evaluated. We report the sealed design, execution accounting, the preregistered Mininet 10% holdout (no validator–emulator disagreements observed), and an artifact‑grounded discussion of interpretation, methodological tradeoffs, and threats to validity (preregistration id: cnsms2026‑gvr‑effectiveness‑02).

sections.introduction: Automating intent→configuration translation with generative language models promises operational efficiency but risks incorrect or unsafe network changes that can cause outages or policy violations. To mitigate these risks, many systems combine generation with deterministic validators and repair loops (generate–validate–repair, GVR). However, the operational benefit of automated repair depends on baseline prevalence of validator‑detectable failures, validator coverage, and the repair budget/effectiveness. We preregistered a narrowly scoped confirmatory question: Does an automated, deterministic GVR pipeline that consults a deterministic NetOps validator materially reduce validator‑detected unsafe or semantically incorrect network changes relative to an LLM‑only generation pipeline on a curated 200‑task intent→configuration bank? The study uses a paired design that fixes the generator output per task to isolate the marginal effect of invoking validation and (if needed) a single repair prompt on the identical candidate.
sections.related_work: Prior work documents LLM factual errors, prompt sensitivity, and non‑determinism, and proposes mitigation patterns including grounding (RAG), verifier‑assisted repair, and guarded agent architectures. NetOps prototypes demonstrate intent→configuration feasibility but rarely provide instrumented, preregistered failure‑rate measurements under controlled causal contrasts between generation and GVR. Red‑team and tool‑injection studies further highlight configuration‑level brittleness and expanded attack surfaces for agentic workflows. Our study situates itself as an externally auditable, preregistered measurement that isolates the marginal effect of deterministic validator‑assisted repair for a fixed model and fixed generation policy.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and primary estimand. We preregistered the confirmatory plan (cnsms2026‑gvr‑effectiveness‑02): a paired design with n = 200 tasks, one shared deterministic initial generation per task, and up to one automated repair call per task. The primary estimand was the paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline; the primary test was an exact two‑sided McNemar test (α = 0.05). Bootstrap percentile CIs were computed with 10,000 resamples (bootstrap_seed = 1729).

Task bank and validators. The benchmark is a curated machine‑checkable intent→configuration bank (200 tasks across four topology clusters) where each task encodes initial/final states, workflow constraints, and required sequences. The primary oracle is a deterministic NetOps checker that enforces syntactic and intent/constraint rules and emits structured diagnostics (valid flag, violation codes, parsed versus required command counts). A Mininet‑based data‑plane emulator was preregistered as an independent disagreement detector applied to a randomized 10% holdout to reveal validator blind spots.

Adapter semantics and determinism clarification (required revision). The run used an adapter that enforces shared_initial generation semantics: for each task a single generator output was deterministically produced and reused for both baseline and guarded conditions. This design choice isolates the marginal effect of validation/repair on the same candidate and intentionally excludes gains from repeated sampling. The execution artifacts show a model_configuration artifact where the model parameter "temperature" is not set (listed as null) and an adapter/accounting artifact that records a single hosted generation per task and stage counts identifying a shared_initial_generation stage. In other words, determinism in this run arose from adapter enforcement of shared_initial semantics (single shared invocation per task) rather than from setting an explicit model temperature parameter in the model call. The adapter/accounting fields and the reconciliation artifact therefore substantiate that each task had one audited model invocation reused across conditions.

Repair policy, budgeting, and contamination handling. The preregistered repair policy allowed at most one automated repair prompt when the primary validator reported violations; any repaired candidate would be re‑validated. The plan limited total model calls to 400 (200 initial + up to 200 repairs); adapter enforcement prevented exceeding that cap. The contamination plan required the Mininet holdout to detect any validator–emulator disagreement; pairs flagged for disagreement were to be excluded from the primary analysis. The execution produced a contamination summary for the holdout indicating no disagreements were detected. We note an explicit reproducibility limitation: the labeled artifact set does not include the randomized selection seed that determined which tasks comprised the 10% Mininet holdout; that missing seed prevents bit‑for‑bit reconstruction of the exact holdout draw even though the contamination summary reports zero disagreements.

Randomization, seeds, and reproducibility. Task ordering and example generator seeds were fixed as recorded in the benchmark manifest. The bootstrap CI procedure used the recorded bootstrap_seed. All model calls, validator traces, and analysis artifacts were archived. For auditability we identify the canonical archived artifacts that substantiate the key methodological facts reported here (adapter enforcement of shared_initial semantics and accounting, model configuration metadata, and the analysis contingency summaries); these artifact names are available in the archived execution bundle and were used to produce the confirmatory analysis.
sections.results:
Execution accounting. The run completed all planned episodes. Accounting summary: completed_pair_count = 200; total model calls used = 200 (one shared initial generation per task); repair calls used = 0; no technical failures affected the primary analysis. Adapter accounting recorded a single audited generation per task under the shared_initial stage, confirming the preregistered shared‑initial semantics.

Validator outcomes and paired inference. Every initial candidate passed the primary deterministic validator: baseline_success_count = 200/200 and guarded_success_count = 200/200. The paired contingency table is n11 = 200, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. With no discordant pairs the observed paired difference = 0.0. The prespecified exact McNemar two‑sided test yields p = 1.0. Bootstrap percentile confidence intervals (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729) produce a 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0]. Under the preregistered estimand and test the preregistered ≥50% relative reduction hypothesis is not evaluable because baseline validator failures were absent.

Repairs, contamination holdout, and secondary outcomes. Because no validator failures occurred, the repair branch was not invoked and secondary estimands (repair iteration statistics, GVR‑introduced failure rates, model‑call cost per repair) are empty for this run. The randomized 10% Mininet holdout executed as preregistered and the contamination summary reports zero validator–emulator disagreements for that holdout sample; however, exact deterministic reconstruction of that holdout draw is impeded by the missing labeled selection seed (see Methods). Representative validator traces confirm that generated sequences matched each task’s required_sequence and that validator diagnostics indicated zero violations for exercised difficulty patterns.
sections.discussion:
Conditional interpretation. The artifact‑grounded null outcome is precise and reproducible within the archived bundle for the chosen design: every generator output passed the primary validator, so there were no validator‑detectable failures for GVR to reduce. This does not imply that GVR is generically useless; rather, the marginal value of automated repair depends on baseline validator failure prevalence and validator coverage for the workload and generation policy in use.

Why the null occurred. The benchmark tasks encode explicit workflow constraints and the primary validator enforces them; archived validator diagnostics show parsed_command_count matching required_command_count for the produced outputs. Difficulty labels indicate the benchmark included nontrivial dependency patterns, so the generator/prompt pair produced correct sequences under the frozen policy. Adapter enforcement of a single shared generation per task removed sampling variance as a pathway to producing alternative (possibly failing) candidates, so the paired contrast isolated only validator+repair effects on that fixed candidate.

Methodological tradeoffs. The paired shared‑initial design improves internal control but excludes benefits obtainable by resampling the LLM (e.g., generating alternative candidates that might fail or be repairable). For unconditional operational failure‑rate estimation and for measuring repair effectiveness in practice, designs with independent multi‑sample draws per condition, nonzero temperature sampling, larger repair budgets, or model ensembles will be necessary.

Validator coverage and emulator corroboration. Deterministic validators are necessary but not sufficient oracles for operational safety. The Mininet holdout provides an independent data‑plane check and found no disagreements in the sampled 10% holdout; because the holdout draw seed is not labeled in the artifacts, that corroboration is informative but its exact deterministic reproducibility is limited. Operational assurance should therefore include richer validator models, larger emulation sampling, adversarial perturbations, and selected real‑device checks.

Practical recommendations. Before committing engineering effort to automated repair, practitioners should measure baseline validator failure prevalence on representative generation policies and assess validator completeness via emulation or selective real‑device checks. Where baseline validator failures are rare, resource allocation toward expanding validator fidelity, adversarial testing, or introducing multi‑sample generation to surface latent failures may yield higher marginal safety returns than single‑step automated repair under a shared‑initial regime.
sections.conclusion: We preregistered and executed a sealed paired study comparing LLM‑only generation to a deterministic GVR pipeline on 200 NetOps intent→configuration tasks using gpt‑5‑mini and a deterministic validator. Both pipelines produced validator‑passing configurations for every task (n11 = 200; no discordant pairs), yielding an observed paired difference of 0.0, exact McNemar p = 1.0, and bootstrap 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0]. The preregistered ≥50% relative‑reduction hypothesis could not be evaluated because baseline validator failures were absent under the frozen shared‑initial generation policy. The results are artifact‑grounded and conditionally informative: automated repair’s marginal value depends on baseline failure prevalence and validator coverage. Future preregistered studies should target workloads with nontrivial baseline failure rates, expand validator fidelity and emulation sampling, record holdout selection seeds to ensure reconstruction, and evaluate multi‑sample and multi‑model policies and multi‑step repair budgets.

disclosure_statement: Disclosure (mandatory). The run executed under preregistration id cnsms2026‑gvr‑effectiveness‑02. Declared model: gpt‑5‑mini (provider label: openai_responses) invoked via the hosted_netops_gvr_v1 adapter. The exact initial master prompt is archived at the required provenance reference (provenance/master_prompt.txt) with SHA‑256: 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba. Topic constraints: the human Research Director limited the study to Generative AI and LLMs for NetOps focusing on safety/reliability of generated network changes. Orchestration and artifacts: the experiment used the hosted_netops_gvr_v1 adapter, deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5 for task generation, and deterministic_netops_validator_v5 as the primary validator. Preregistration/freeze: study design (paired estimand, sample size n = 200, shared‑initial generation semantics, stopping rules, maximum model calls = 400, repair budget = 1 per task) was frozen before any model calls. Determinism note (clarification required by reviewers): model configuration metadata lists the model parameter "temperature" as unset (null) in the archived model configuration; runtime determinism was achieved by adapter enforcement of a single audited shared_initial generation per task (adapter/accounting and reconciliation artifacts record a single hosted generation per task and stage_counts indicating shared_initial_generation). Model calls and adapter accounting were audited and archived; these artifacts substantiate that each task had one audited generation reused across both conditions. Execution accounting: the autonomous run executed (start and end timestamps archived) and used 200 model calls (one shared initial generation per task); up to 200 repair calls were allowed but none were invoked because every initial candidate passed the primary validator. Contamination check: a Mininet‑based emulator was preregistered and executed on a randomized 10% holdout as an independent disagreement detector; the archived contamination summary reports zero disagreements in that holdout. Known reproducibility gap (required by reviewers): the labeled artifact set does not include the explicit randomized selection seed used to draw the 10% Mininet holdout, which prevents exact deterministic reconstruction of the holdout draw despite the reported zero disagreements. Human involvement: the human Research Director selected the topic family and pre‑lock constraints; no human manual editing or selective rewriting of technical manuscript content occurred after the autonomy lock. No post‑preregistration design changes or technical restarts occurred.
limitations: Task‑bank scope: the confirmatory sample used a curated synthetic/public intent→configuration bank (n = 200); results reflect this bank and may not generalize to broader production workloads or adversarial distributions.

Single‑model and shared‑initial setting: only gpt‑5‑mini (hosted) with adapter‑enforced shared_initial generation was tested. Outcomes may differ across model families, independent per‑condition sampling, nonzero temperature sampling, or larger repair budgets.

Validator coverage: the deterministic validator enforces a defined set of syntax and intent checks and cannot capture all device idiosyncrasies or emergent failure modes detectable only by richer emulation or real‑device execution.

Adversarial robustness untested: this confirmatory run did not perform active adversarial injections or red‑team tool‑description attacks; prior audits indicate such vectors can bypass naive defenses and require separate evaluation.

Reproducibility gap for contamination check: the randomized holdout selection seed for the Mininet contamination check is not present in the labeled artifacts, preventing exact reconstruction of the holdout selection.

Single repair budget: the GVR pipeline allowed at most one automated repair prompt per task; multi‑step repair strategies, iterative repair budgets, or human‑in‑the‑loop escalation were not exercised here.
